name: Jade Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. I'll keep this confidential. What happens on an ordinary day at your desk?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I arrive at North Window Accounts with a lunch box and a list of client questions I did not finish yesterday. I'm 43, a junior accountant with a bachelor's degree in accounting; I still ask the senior to check tax allowances because I can miss a change in the rules. I like when a school or small charity can see where its money went, and I dislike the buzzing queue of forms by three o'clock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and what do savings and technology look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Dev repairs lifts, and we have two children in primary school and a mortgage. My pay is typical for this accounting role, we have four months of expenses saved, and there are some similar firms nearby. I do not use AI tools; I prefer checking a paper trail with the senior beside me, and new software makes me worry I'll miss an error. I support unions and stronger rules for employers, because a worker should not learn about a lost job from a blank rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues a faster form sorter is fine if it keeps a clear record of what it changed. I would ask that the senior still checks the school accounts before they go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job probably stays, but I'm a junior who still needs help with tax changes and we have a mortgage. Four months saved keeps me from losing sleep every night, though one bad review could still affect my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the paper trail and ask the senior to review my school returns as usual. In the first year I'd add fifty a month to the mortgage reserve and bring any new sorter to the staff meeting before it reaches client files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than calm. The household is steady, but my junior place is not the strongest chair in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say in that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show us the record of what the sorter changed, and let a reviewer check the first batch. I would not ask others to reject it; I just want the audit trail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the fifty come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could keep our old television and skip the instalment plan for a new one. Dev and I can make that small saving without touching the children's lunches.

I would keep a **senior review** on school accounts.
think: My **job likely stays**, but I remain a junior needing help.
The **mortgage** makes a bad review or lost hours matter.
do: Keep checking **school returns** with the senior and paper records.
Save **fifty monthly** by skipping a new television instalment.
Raise the **sorter audit trail** at the staff meeting.
feel: She feels **uneasy** because her junior place is still insecure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff meeting that the firm must give people paid time to learn whatever it brings in. I would ask who is going to check the school accounts when the software says they are finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking, writing explanations and answering clients are much of my job, and I am still learning them. I expect the partners to cut junior hours first, and Dev's lift repairs alone would not carry the mortgage and two children's costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff group for a written guarantee of paid training hours and notice before any roster cut. In the first year of steady change, if my hours fall below four days a week, I'd apply for advertised payroll-clerk roles at the hospital and two nearby firms while keeping any paid work here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about my own hours. Four months saved would not last long against the loan and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new software in training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sit through a paid demonstration on old files if it is required, but I would not use AI on a live return on my own. I need a person to show me what it misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask to come with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the other junior, Lila, to bring the hours log to the staff meeting. A rota is harder to deny when two junior accountants have written down their hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell North Window's staff that full AGI in 2028 reaches the paperwork we do now, and no one should hide the likely cuts. I would ask for a proper staff consultation and a rule on who signs a machine-prepared return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My desk work can be done by AGI in 2028, and robots around 2031 do not buy me three more years. I expect my junior post to go; Dev's lift repairs may be hit by robots later, so we could lose both wages in stages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add one hundred monthly to our mortgage reserve by putting the summer trip on hold, and ask the staff group to demand written notice and paid redeployment help. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply for posted salaried school finance roles and draw on savings only for bills while Dev keeps working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. Four months of savings would not protect a mortgage if both careers change within a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are visiting the nearby park this summer instead of taking the train away. The children may complain, but the mortgage money must stay put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use public support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lost the job and qualified for help with the mortgage, I would apply while searching for paid work. I have paid into that system, and I would not call using it a failure.

I would ask for **paid redeployment** instead of vague retraining promises.
think: My **junior desk post** may go when AGI takes the checking work in 2028.

Apply for **posted school finance** jobs if my post ends after 2028.
Apply for **mortgage support** only after job loss and if eligible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for a union agreement on paid moves and for the firm to tell us what happens to junior jobs. I would still want the accountant who checks a school return named.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, I would still have a mortgage and children to support. AGI could do the checking I am finally getting better at, while robots might reach Dev's hands-on lift work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the staff group's proposal for paid school-finance training next year and add fifty monthly to our reserve while both wages hold. In the first year after 2031, if North Window cuts my hours, I'd apply for posted salaried school bursar jobs and keep my paid accounting shifts until I have a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, with time to plan but no promise that a school will hire me. Five years of pay would help us keep the mortgage current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the training need to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A school's budget calendar, grant reports and the deadline for paying staff. I would attend if it happens during paid hours; I cannot give up wages to sit in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses the proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep doing the returns and ask the union representative to put the refusal in the meeting record. Then I would look at actual school vacancies, not buy a course myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives employers time to make a fair agreement with staff rather than drop junior posts in one year. The firm could keep a paper record clients can question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, our children may be grown, but the mortgage may still be there. If we can keep both wages for a decade, we could pay much of it down before AGI reaches my desk; Dev's lift work might face robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union representative to seek a paid route into school accounts and keep adding fifty a month to mortgage principal while both wages hold. In the first year after 2036, if the junior post ends, I'd take a posted salaried school finance role only with a written wage offer; otherwise I'd keep any paid hours and apply for support if eligible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than alarmed here. A decade of wages would make the loan smaller, but at 53 I would still need a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early if the loan gets small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our four months saved today is not a pension. I would rather keep earning and let the children see that a worker can change jobs without being thrown away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to put in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid training hours, notice of junior cuts and a named reviewer on school accounts. I want a signed staff agreement that a new firm partner cannot simply forget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior post could disappear before we have paid down the mortgage. A signed staff agreement, paid school-finance training and a real salaried vacancy would help. The family cannot live on a promise to retrain later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a school finds a wrong number after a machine says the accounts are done. Someone must be able to point to the source paper and explain it to parents.

headlineQuote: The family cannot live on a promise to retrain later.
portrait: Jade, **43**, is a junior accountant with an accounting bachelor’s degree, still learning school and charity returns.
Her **typical pay** supports two children and a mortgage with Dev, while four months saved and some nearby firms offer limited room.
She **never uses AI** and insists on a paper trail, human checks and a staff voice before new software.
Her main fear is **2028 job loss**; with more time she seeks signed paid training, school work and mortgage reduction.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior job before the family reduces its mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A **signed staff agreement**, paid school-finance training and a real salaried vacancy would help.
